theme: Submission; suffering for righteousness; Christ’s example
readingInstruction: Read 1 Peter 2:13-3:22. Peter applies the gospel to life under authority: citizens, servants, wives, husbands, and the whole church. Notice that Christ is the pattern in every relationship and that suffering for doing good is a calling.
settingTheScene: Christians in Asia Minor were slandered as lawless, antisocial, and subversive. Peter does not tell them to withdraw from society. He tells them to live so well that the accusations fall flat. The “household codes” in this section (similar to those in Ephesians 5-6 and Colossians 3) were not new in the ancient world, but Peter grounds them in Christ’s example. Many of the servants and wives he addresses were in difficult situations, and he points them to the Suffering Servant.
observation: “Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution” (2:13).
“Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor” (2:17).
“For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps” (2:21).
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness” (2:24).
“Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless” (3:9).
“But in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you” (3:15).
“For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God’s will, than for doing evil” (3:17).
“Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (3:18).
interpretation:
Peter first addresses believers as citizens: “Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors.” Government exists to punish wrongdoing and praise those who do good. “Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God.” Then four short commands: “Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.” Honor goes to all, but fear belongs to God alone. This does not mean unlimited submission; when the state demands what God forbids, we must obey God (Acts 5:29).

Next he speaks to household servants: be subject to your masters with all respect, even to the unjust. Why? “For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.” Then Peter describes the Suffering Servant in the words of Isaiah 53. “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed. For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.” The cross is both an example and an atonement: first Christ is our substitute, and only then our model. We cannot imitate what we have not received.

Chapter 3 turns to marriage. Wives are to be subject to their own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, “they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives.” Their beauty is to be that of “the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious.” Husbands are to live with their wives “in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.” Husbands and wives are equal heirs. Christians differ on how to apply the language of submission: complementarians see a distinct role of loving headship and willing submission rooted in creation, while egalitarians stress mutual submission and see the instruction as addressing a cultural setting. All agree that Peter calls both to humble, honoring love, and that abuse is never permissible.

Then the whole church: “have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind.” Return blessing for insult. Do not fear what they fear, “but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect.” Notice that the world asks about our hope when it sees us respond well to suffering. Keep a good conscience, “for it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God’s will, than for doing evil.”

The ground of it is Christ: “For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.” The next verses (3:19-22) are among the hardest in the New Testament. Who are the “spirits in prison” to whom Christ proclaimed? Some think the fallen angels of Genesis 6 (as in 1 Enoch), to whom the risen Christ announced his victory; some think the people of Noah’s day, to whom Christ preached through Noah by his Spirit; and some think Christ descended to the dead. Likewise, “Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you” has been taken in different ways: as the outward sign that points to the inward reality, as an appeal to God for a good conscience, or as a means of grace. All agree that it is Christ’s resurrection that saves, and that he is now at God’s right hand, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to him.
connection: Romans 13:1-7 speaks of governing authorities, and Acts 4:19 and 5:29 show the limit. Isaiah 53:4-12 is behind 2:22-25. Ephesians 5:22-33 and Colossians 3:18-4:1 are the parallel household codes. Genesis 6:1-4 and Jude 6 touch on the spirits in prison. Genesis 6-8 is the account of Noah. 1 Peter 4:6 mentions the gospel preached to the dead. Romans 6:3-4 and Colossians 2:11-12 speak of baptism. Matthew 5:38-48 teaches blessing enemies. Psalm 34:12-16 is quoted in 3:10-12. Hebrews 1:3 and Ephesians 1:20-22 say Christ is at the right hand.
application:
Think of a person in authority over you whom you find hard to respect. Ask how you can honor them as unto the Lord, and how you can pray for them.

Rehearse 3:15 so you are ready to explain your hope to someone who asks. Write out a two-minute answer.

If you are married, ask your spouse how you can show them honor this week.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for not reviling in return when he was reviled.
Thank him for bearing your sins.
Ask him to help you suffer well when you suffer for doing right.
